title: Trump Posthumously Pardons Clarence Olin Freeman for Illegal Whiskey Case
description_medium: Trump issued a posthumous pardon to Clarence Olin Freeman on January 19, 2021, for a 1965 South Carolina case involving conspiracy to violate interstate revenue laws and illegal whiskey. Freeman was sentenced to nine months in prison and five years’ probation. The White House said he later led a law-abiding life and built a business and community ties. The pardon came more than five decades after conviction.
description_long:
President Donald Trump granted a posthumous pardon to Clarence Olin Freeman on January 19, 2021. Freeman had been convicted in the District of South Carolina in 1965 of conspiracy to violate interstate revenue laws and offenses involving dealing in and possessing illegal whiskey. The Justice Department lists a sentence of nine months in prison and five years of probation. The White House described the case as operating an illegal whiskey still.

Freeman had died before the pardon was issued, making the grant posthumous. The White House said that after his release he led a law-abiding life, built a stable marriage and a successful business, and contributed to his community. The pardon forgave the old federal conviction; it did not alter the historical case. The unusual timing and the decades between sentence and pardon are central to the event. The official clemency statement and index support the case, sentence and posthumous nature, while the biographical details are the White House’s account.
evidence_notes: Official White House confirms 1965 illegal still case and post-conviction account; DOJ-index/master warrant confirms sentence and that pardon was posthumous.
corrected_wording: Corrected title to: Trump Posthumously Pardons Clarence Olin Freeman for Illegal Whiskey Case

title: Trump Posthumously Pardons Steven Samuel Grantham for 1967 Stolen-Car Conviction
description_medium: Trump issued a posthumous pardon to Steven Samuel Grantham on January 19, 2021, for a 1967 conviction involving interstate transportation of a stolen vehicle. DOJ records four months in prison and two years of supervised release. The White House said Grantham was convicted of stealing a vehicle. He had died before the pardon; the official record gives no further case-specific conduct or reason for clemency.
description_long:
On January 19, 2021, President Donald Trump granted a posthumous pardon to Steven Samuel Grantham. The Justice Department identifies his conviction in the Central District of California as interstate transportation of a stolen vehicle and lists a sentence of four months in prison and two years of supervised release, imposed in 1967. The White House summarized the offense as stealing a vehicle.

Grantham had died before the pardon was granted. The master warrant for the January 19 grants identifies the pardon as posthumous, distinguishing it from the pardons of other recipients on the same list. No public source reviewed here establishes what vehicle was involved, Grantham’s precise role or why the pardon was sought. The grant forgave the old federal conviction but did not change the historical record. The supported account is therefore the decades-old stolen-car case, its short sentence and the posthumous clemency action.
evidence_notes: Master warrant confirms posthumous grant; DOJ clemency index supplies charge and 1967 sentence.
corrected_wording: Corrected title to: Trump Posthumously Pardons Steven Samuel Grantham for 1967 Stolen-Car Conviction

title: Trump Pardons North Carolina Hunter James E. Johnson Jr.
description_medium: Trump pardoned James E. Johnson Jr. on January 19, 2021, for federal wildlife offenses in North Carolina. DOJ lists hunting over bait and aiding and abetting that conduct, as well as killing a migratory game bird without keeping it in his actual custody. Johnson received one year of probation and a $7,500 fine in 2008. Public records reviewed here provide no further detail on the hunt or species.
description_long:
President Donald Trump granted a full pardon to James E. Johnson Jr. on January 19, 2021, for federal hunting offenses in the Eastern District of North Carolina. The Justice Department lists hunting over bait and aiding and abetting that offense, as well as killing a migratory game bird without retaining it in actual custody. Johnson was sentenced in 2008 to one year of probation and a $7,500 fine.

Federal wildlife regulations restrict hunting migratory birds over bait because feeding can concentrate birds and make them easier to kill. The public clemency record does not identify the hunt’s location, species, number of birds or Johnson’s precise role. The pardon forgave the federal convictions but did not expunge the court history. With no case-specific narrative available in the sources reviewed, those particulars should not be supplied. The documented event is a clemency grant for a wildlife-law conviction, with the offense and penalty recorded in the official index.
evidence_notes: DOJ clemency index establishes counts and sentence; no event-specific hunting account located to identify species/location.
corrected_wording: Corrected title to: Trump Pardons North Carolina Hunter James E. Johnson Jr.

title: Paper Scrap Catches on Trump’s Shoe While Boarding Air Force One
description_medium: On October 4, 2018, a piece of white paper caught on Donald Trump’s shoe as he boarded Air Force One at Minneapolis–Saint Paul International Airport. The New York Post said it could have been toilet paper, a napkin or another scrap; Yahoo reported it as toilet paper. Photographs and video showed the paper trailing from his shoe. The brief incident drew online jokes, but its exact material was not established.
description_long:
As President Donald Trump boarded Air Force One at Minneapolis–Saint Paul International Airport on October 4, 2018, a piece of white paper became caught on the sole of one shoe and trailed behind him up the stairs. Photographs and video of the moment circulated widely and prompted jokes online. The New York Post reported that the scrap looked like toilet paper but said it might have been a napkin or another piece of paper; Yahoo’s report identified it as toilet paper.

That difference matters: the footage shows a loose paper scrap, but does not establish what it was. The sources also reported that a staff member retrieved it after the plane’s door was closed. The episode was a brief visual mishap during a public departure, not a policy event. A careful description can state where and when it happened and why it attracted attention while preserving the uncertainty over the paper’s identity. The available reporting does not establish how long Trump was unaware of it.
evidence_notes: Corrected categorical identification: the footage shows paper, while sources differed whether it was toilet paper or a napkin. Avoided unsupported claim he was unaware for minutes.
corrected_wording: Corrected title to: Paper Scrap Catches on Trump’s Shoe While Boarding Air Force One

title: Trump Pardons Hal Knudson Mergler for 1992 LSD Conviction
description_medium: Trump granted Hal Knudson Mergler a full pardon on January 19, 2021, for a 1992 conspiracy conviction involving possession and distribution of LSD. DOJ lists one month in prison, three years of supervised release and $505 restitution. The White House said Mergler later earned a college degree, built a business and helped build a school for a nonprofit. The pardon was supported by Rod Rosenstein and the Office of the Pardon Attorney.
description_long:
President Donald Trump granted a full pardon to Hal Knudson Mergler on January 19, 2021, for a 1992 federal conviction involving conspiracy to possess with intent to distribute and distribute LSD. The Justice Department records a sentence of one month in prison, three years of supervised release and $505 restitution. The offense was in the Northern District of West Virginia.

The White House said Mergler later earned a college degree, built a successful business career, started a family and helped build a school for a nonprofit charitable organization. It identified former Deputy Attorney General Rod Rosenstein and the Office of the Pardon Attorney as supporters of clemency. The pardon forgave the conviction but did not erase the historical court record. The public sources do not detail the 1992 distribution conduct, so the account focuses on the documented offense and sentence alongside the later life described in the official pardon announcement.
evidence_notes: Corrected generic record with the White House’s recipient-specific rehabilitation and supporters account; DOJ confirms original offense and sentence.
corrected_wording: Corrected title to: Trump Pardons Hal Knudson Mergler for 1992 LSD Conviction

title: Trump Pardons Mortgage Broker Benedict Guthrie Olberding for Bank Fraud
description_medium: Trump pardoned Benedict Guthrie Olberding on January 19, 2021, for bank fraud in South Carolina. DOJ records five years of probation and $614,154.37 in restitution. Olberding was a mortgage broker who pleaded guilty after arranging a fraudulent loan related to the sale of a Murrells Inlet home with a co-defendant. The public clemency index does not explain the pardon rationale.
description_long:
On January 19, 2021, President Donald Trump granted a full pardon to Benedict Guthrie Olberding, a mortgage broker convicted of bank fraud in the District of South Carolina. The Justice Department records five years of probation and $614,154.37 in restitution, imposed in 2013. A state financial regulator’s later consent order notes Olberding had pleaded guilty in 2011 to a felony bank-fraud count. Contemporary local coverage tied the case to a property sale in Murrells Inlet involving co-defendant Joseph Guernsey.

The pardon forgave the federal conviction but did not remove the restitution obligation from the historical sentence or erase the case. The available public sources reviewed here provide only limited detail about the transaction and the precise false information used, so the description avoids stating a broader mortgage scheme or a loss beyond the recorded restitution. The clemency index confirms the grant and sentence, while the regulatory and local records support the mortgage-broker context.
evidence_notes: Corrected generic entry with state regulator record and contemporaneous local report tied to same defendant/case; avoided overclaiming scheme details.
corrected_wording: Corrected title to: Trump Pardons Mortgage Broker Benedict Guthrie Olberding for Bank Fraud

title: Trump Administration Diverts $3.8 Billion in Pentagon Funds to Border Wall
description_medium: After Congress declined the requested wall funding, the Trump administration redirected billions from military construction and other Defense Department accounts to build sections of the U.S.–Mexico border wall. A September 2019 transfer affected 127 projects; in February 2020, the Pentagon announced another $3.8 billion diversion. Critics challenged the transfers under appropriations law, while the administration relied on emergency authorities. Reporting described postponed projects, not a literal theft or permanent cancellation of every project.
description_long:
After Congress provided less border-wall funding than President Donald Trump sought, his administration redirected Defense Department money to border-barrier construction. In September 2019, the Pentagon identified $3.6 billion in military construction funds for wall projects, affecting 127 projects in the United States and abroad. In February 2020, the Defense Department announced an additional $3.8 billion transfer from other accounts, including procurement and research funds, to support wall construction.

The transfers drew legal challenges over whether the executive branch could use emergency authorities to redirect funds Congress had appropriated for other purposes. The Supreme Court allowed construction to proceed while litigation continued; that procedural decision did not resolve every dispute over the administration’s authority. The diverted funds meant that planned military projects were deferred or lost their scheduled funding, though the status of each project varied. Calling the action a “theft” overstates what the cited reporting established. The central dispute concerned presidential discretion over appropriations and the practical trade-offs for military construction, rather than proof of criminal taking.
evidence_notes: Corrected title’s theft claim and distinguished Sept. 2019 $3.6B construction transfer from Feb. 2020 additional $3.8B transfer. Legal approval described only as interim construction relief.
corrected_wording: Corrected title to: Trump Administration Diverts $3.8 Billion in Pentagon Funds to Border Wall

title: Trump Commutes Arkansas Operator Theodore “Ted” Suhl’s Bribery Sentence
description_medium: Trump commuted Theodore E. “Ted” Suhl’s sentence on July 29, 2019, for bribery and honest-services fraud involving an Arkansas Medicaid official. Suhl owned juvenile mental-health providers and sought to have Medicaid cases steered to his company through payments to an official, using an intermediary. He had been sentenced to 84 months in prison, three years of supervised release and a $200,000 fine. The commutation reduced imprisonment without vacating his conviction.
description_long:
On July 29, 2019, President Donald Trump commuted the prison sentence of Theodore E. “Ted” Suhl, a former operator of juvenile mental-health treatment businesses in Arkansas. A federal jury had convicted Suhl of honest-services fraud and bribery-related offenses. The Eighth Circuit described evidence that Suhl intended for a state official to divert juvenile Medicaid cases to one of Suhl’s companies; payments passed through an intermediary. The companies provided inpatient and outpatient care to young people and received Medicaid reimbursements.

The Justice Department records an 84-month prison term, three years of supervised release and a $200,000 fine. A commutation changes punishment, not the conviction itself; Trump’s action reduced Suhl’s custodial sentence while leaving the other components in place. The clemency was supported by former Arkansas governor Mike Huckabee and former U.S. attorney Bud Cummins, according to contemporaneous reporting. The case involved a business seeking public-program referrals through bribery, rather than a technical billing mistake. Court opinions and DOJ records support the case facts and sentence; no broader conclusion about the treatment centers is needed to explain the commutation.
evidence_notes: Corrected generic entry with DOJ and appellate case details. Preserved that the action was a commutation, not a pardon.
corrected_wording: Corrected title to: Trump Commutes Arkansas Operator Theodore “Ted” Suhl’s Bribery Sentence

title: Trump Commutes Florida Resort-Fraud Sentence of Fred Davis Clark Jr.
description_medium: Trump commuted Fred Davis Clark Jr.’s prison sentence on January 13, 2021, for his role in a $300 million Cay Clubs vacation-property fraud. Clark was convicted of bank fraud and false statements to financial institutions and sentenced to 40 years. Prosecutors said resort-unit sales to insiders were funded with company money to create false demand and inflate prices. The commutation left five years of supervised release and nearly $179.1 million in restitution in place.
description_long:
President Donald Trump commuted Fred Davis Clark Jr.’s prison sentence on January 13, 2021, for his role as chief executive and majority owner of Cay Clubs Resorts and Marinas. A jury convicted Clark in 2015 of bank fraud and making false statements to financial institutions in a scheme involving purported vacation-resort units. Prosecutors said Cay Clubs used company money to finance purchases by insiders, then presented those transactions as genuine market demand to attract investors. The Department of Justice described a roughly $300 million fraud affecting about 1,400 investors.

Clark was sentenced in 2016 to 40 years in prison. The Justice Department’s commutation warrant reduced the prison term to time served, while leaving five years of supervised release and the remaining sentence components, including restitution, intact. The listed restitution exceeded $179 million. The clemency therefore ended the incarceration portion but did not vacate the conviction or cancel the financial judgment. The case is a useful example of the scale of the alleged investor losses and the terms preserved after commutation.
evidence_notes: DOJ trial/sentencing press release documents the scheme and investors; commutation warrant specifies time served and intact supervised release/sentence components.
corrected_wording: Corrected title to: Trump Commutes Florida Resort-Fraud Sentence of Fred Davis Clark Jr.

title: Trump Commutes Jonathan Braun’s Marijuana-Smuggling Sentence
description_medium: Trump commuted Jonathan Braun’s 10-year federal sentence on January 19, 2021, releasing him after about a year in custody while leaving five years of supervised release and a $100,000 fine intact. Braun pleaded guilty to importing marijuana and money laundering and was described by prosecutors as a high-ranking member of a cross-border smuggling operation. The commutation did not pardon the convictions.
description_long:
On January 19, 2021, President Donald Trump commuted Jonathan Braun’s prison sentence for conspiracy to import marijuana into the United States and money laundering. Braun had been sentenced in 2019 to ten years in prison, five years of supervised release and a $100,000 fine. He had served about a year when Trump’s commutation reduced the prison term to time served. The warrant left the supervised-release term and other components of the sentence intact.

Federal prosecutors described Braun as a high-ranking member of an international marijuana-smuggling operation that moved large quantities from Canada into the United States. The Justice Department records the convictions and sentence but does not state a public rationale for the commutation. The action reduced incarceration; it did not erase the conviction or absolve the money-laundering offense. This distinction is important because “commutation” can be mistaken for a full pardon. Reporting since his release has focused on separate alleged and proven violations of supervised release, but those later cases are distinct from the 2021 clemency grant and are not necessary to establish what Trump changed.
evidence_notes: DOJ index and warrant establish sentence and preserved supervision; AP details scale/role and later events as separate proceedings.
corrected_wording: Corrected title to: Trump Commutes Jonathan Braun’s Marijuana-Smuggling Sentence
